newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's Iliescu woos workers in polls showdown.
newsitem.headline: Romania's Iliescu woos workers in polls showdown.

text.p: Romanian President Ion Iliescu, an ex-communist. told sceptical factory workers on Friday that the reformist rival he faces in a tough re-election fight would rob them of their homes and bring back the king.

Touring a shipyard and a vast steel mill, a hard hat perched on his head, Iliescu asked workers to back him in the November 17 run-off against centrist Emil Constantinescu or risk instability and chaos under a modernising government.
Iliescu, in power since the 1989 revoliution which toppled Stalinisyt dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, won the first round of the presidential election last Sunday.

He finished four points ahead of Constantinescu -- a professor with no political career under communism -- whose reformists won elections to parliament, throwing Iliescu's leftist party out of power for the first time.

"Constantinescu has acquired no experience in parliament and has never worked in administration. He learns his lessons, but sometimes badly," Iliescu told some of the Sidex steel mill's 35,000 workers in the River Danube port of Galati.
"I'm close to the problems of workers. My father was a worker. I trained at an industrial school. I know what physical work means."

Iliescu's opponents, anxious to implement a programme to alleviate the mass poverty they blame on his cautious reforms, say Romania cannot emerge fully from its communist past unless the president is voted out of office.
Constantinescu got an important boost this week when the third-place finisher in the first round, former prime minister Petre Roman, threw his support behind him in the run-off.
Galati, a showcase of communist-era industry, went into decline after Ceausescu's execution in 1989. The town gave Iliescu a polite, but far from rousing, reception.
Local shipyard workers, with average monthly pay of $100, stood in silence on scaffolding to hear Iliescu speak from a platform, his voice occasionally overpowered by a warning horn.
"I can't possibly buy a home on my pay," one worker told Iliescu. "It's the opposition that's trying to speculate on your troubles," the president replied.
Galati and other industrial towns, once leftwing bastions, put Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR) bloc on top, according to official results of Sunday's vote.
Iliescu, elected in 1990 and 1992, has lost much of his support in Romania's cities and opinion surveys show he relies increasingly on older and less educated rural voters.
He acknowledged his party had been severely censured in the parliamentary poll, but said his re-election remained the sole chance for Romanians to guard against extremes.
"Like a child angry when it is denied things it sees other children have, Romanians were angry. You now have one chance to protect your interests and that is the president," he said.

His rival, he said, had not made clear whether he supported restoration of exiled ex-king Michael or of pre-war property rights -- a sensitive issue among tenants in buildings taken over by Communist authorities.
"Constantinescu wants to return to what Romania had in 1946, to property rights for landowners and to monarchy."
Constantinescu said Iliescu's charges were aimed at gaining votes by sowing distrust among Romanians.
His election would usher in a new era for the impoverished country, Constantinescu said, hailing the coalition with Roman's Social Democrats. "We have a new government. We also need a new president."

"I will do my best to restore the smile on the faces of the Romanians. If it takes sacrifices, political leaders will make them. I'll be the first to set an example by imposing a new style of presidency, based on seriousness and modesty."
